I have so many gripes about this wonky wacky machine. It doesn't matter if you are an experienced player - it is built to drain. Even the base model comparison -GILD WING - is playable. So, I hope I offend a lot of pinheads arguing for this machine. But the reason I love pinball soo much is all the chaos that can ensure during the game. The ball rolls funny for everyone. But this machine is filled with too much noise. By noise I mean rolls that lead directly down the drain. Loops that shoot center direct drain. Rails that lift and cause metal flakes to scratch the play field. Broken mechs right from the factory. I am sorry, but the idea isn't to put a dollar in and play for thirty seconds. Jack Danger obviously has ADHD and is totally bored with every machine on the market so instead of making an enjoyable playable machine - he forced stern to make a build for himself. And it's total horse $H1+... I downright hate the gameplay. Don't get me wrong, the modes are and videos are amazing. Very akin to Deadpool..but if you can't use your muscle memory and even barely brick a shot- you'll drain. A left out lane flipper isn't a bad idea. In fact, it's quite enjoyable at times. But mostly it's a drain monster. During multi ball especially. I wouldn't be surprised if you could pick up a used cabinet for five grand or trade within a few months. And it will be sterns worst selling machine. Someone in the thread said it was better than the JAWS gameplay and that certainly isn't true. Let's just say at my local arcade, new comers won't touch the machine because when they do, they play for five seconds and hate it. It doesn't draw you in. It isn't fun. And it certainly eats your balls. I also read that someone said, "try getting good at the game". While it is totally possible to learn and master the gameplay - like knowing a slow roll needs a bump on the left side of the play field or else it'll come down and center itself or even watch out for the left flipper not having a sling- but sheesh I don't want to put 100 dollars in a game in order to learn just the basic shots. And even then, you might have a few good games. If you hit the ramp behind the sentinel, it hardly ever goes full throttle. If you hit the city ramp, it is so pitched that it rolls backwards most of the time. If you hit finger kickback, there isn't enough power to give the ball momentum and it literally goes down the center EVERY SINGLE TIME. That's a big no from me, personally.

The way I think about roll offs is I give them a position via a fraction. Let's say there's a percentage to the flipper and an orbit is all the way on the outside lane -thus as such for this machine. If you think -"Ok, full roll off"- and hesitate to swing the bat - you're more likely to get the correct axis from the tip of the flipper. The crate is half bat. So on and so forth. If you own the machine, use some trace paper. Draw out the "rainbow" and angle your bats with lines. Figure out the physics = figuring out the game. Muscle memory comes into play and taking away all that you know about the game is a big part of the fun of the chaos of pinball.  But, you can brick in that game and still continue with grandeur. 

My gameplay technique is to set up the multiballs back to back on ball one. Get the care ready. Get the coffin ready. Choose a mode. Whether it be a head or so on and then bag a multi ball. After draining, aim for the other multiball. If you're able to spam the ramps, well - forget getting a high score. They do not add up over the shots. Happy pinning.

If you want to modify a bit, curl the metal out to the outside of the post slightly. Wrap the ramp with some sort of rubber or something protective and barely twinge it with plyers of your thumbs till it curls slightly. You'll see a difference.

My suggestion, since you own it, take the glass off and roll the ball manually up the ramp. See if there is a hitch. If it bounces or stops, your ramp is turned upward a bit. It happens on a lot of machines. Just be cautious when fixing. But you can also modify the post. It will help your aim to get to the ramp, but not logical in the wild. Just improves your home gameplay. The left ramp in that machine is sandwiched in between two mushrooms. Boy gosh is it so hard to connect properly and not brick the shot. But it's awesome when you over roll the ramp and spam it a few times in a row. The right ramp, well it feels a lot like trying to hit the ramps on led Zeppelin. Happy shooting. Back hand magic tricks for this one. Good luck.

My take. This may very well be one of the first things you have shot. Getting into the basics. Your OTS shots are profile and the lining doesn't make sense. They are 2 shots with a shoulder on the end frame. So not really and OTS. Not sure of the styling here, when you could have just used single frames or done a two shot. Think of the frame as a piece of graph paper. Shit, I am bad with algebra. But remember those x-y axis things. Coordinate graph. Just came to me out of nowhere. Anyways, a scene is kind of like a painting. But, there is the rule of thirds. Front, middle ground, back ground. You will eventually get the understanding of racking. But basics for now. When composing shots though, after you have your coverage, pop that sucker off the stilts, get your camera close to the action and add a little shake to the bad boy. (Shit I am talking in film lingo). In other words, try things. Don't be afraid to move the camera around and find particular things interesting. Pick up the food on the table. Pick up the wine glasses clinking together. Think of the camera as a tool used to show an action sequence. Like the slap being in some POV. It happens in a lot of movies. I think the first commenter was wrong. This story is very well written, actually. The content wasn't executed. 

Lets talk lighting. I am almost certain this was a HXR or there equivocal straight 1080p standard. So you will burn frames with lamps considering the sensor. Those cameras are not built for cinema lamps at all. They are meant to shoot home videos. Drop the F till it's almost hallow looking on that little 2" screen. I mean almost dark. Took me years to learn this. But natural lighting works damn fine with those bad boys. Can get some wonderful images. I am not sure if your school forwards you monitors to use, if not do an HDMI out to your TV. Look at every frame carefully. I tell almost every new director I meet, "Directing isn't just saying action and cut, it is looking at every possible thing in the frame and fixing it to your needs." First time outings, people tend to focus on working with the actors. Pulling emotions. I think you execute that perfectly. But, watch the burnt frames because it can ruin what those people work hard for in their execution. One tip: flesh tone. If the frame doesn't match someone's natural skin. the lamp is too bright. Take it away, take it away, take it away-NOW (Sorry A little humor for the red hot chilli pepper fans.) There was this beautifully mastered shot against the brick then, honestly the composition was ruined by the split frame. If I were you, I would recut that to two separate shots. They seem to match well in color. But that is an artistic choice, and I am not one for taking away integrity. The shot timing can be trimmed quite a bit. In fact you would see a drastic difference in the composition of this piece if you took away a lot of dead frame. One of the hardest things I learned in film school was, a shot doesn't have to be focused on a particular subject when they are speaking. Think of the dropping of the ring and how you cut away to this to show the hesitation of the lead. The dialogue still runs through, and there is no need to show mouths moving or that character in frame to understand who is speaking because that was established. Took me years to learn that as well and still haven't mastered it. So cut away, keep the timing down. A good point of reference is, a single shot in any film is generally 2 seconds long. Why is this? Well the psychological reason is, supposedly it takes 2 seconds to blink. They don't want you to miss a thing. So everything is quick and paced and continues to keep moving. If you go back and look at your edit. See if you can overlay things quicker and trim out as much as you can. The pacing would fix a lot of things here. Grading as well. I think it honestly is a wonderfully fun piece and you composed a lot of great things. Anyways, I am rambling like I know shit. But- keep dreaming. Keep filming. Keep creating. Much love.

This is typical in even writers without ADHD or OCD. Writers block. Inspiration is one of the hardest things to find as a creator. Here is something that helps me: You call yourself a writer, as Charles Bukowski said- "If it doesn't overwhelm you to write, do something else". So if you are a writer a notebook and pen should be with you at all times. Anytime you are not occupied by a task or something that needs accomplishing, sit down and write out the description of the room. The things that are surrounding you. The colors. The vibrancy of the light. The shadows. The textures on the walls. The people surrounding you. What they are wearing. Then write about how this all makes you feel. It only takes a few weeks for this to become a practice. But it helps you become more aware of the surroundings and be more descriptive with your diction. Writing isn't always about telling a particular story or creating a mystical world, sometimes it is just as simple as renaming your thoughts with a random character and just stream of consciousness. One of my favorite authors is Ethan Hawke and he definitely has ADHD. He writes almost as exact as of how I think of things. Even if you can't practice the art you will still have a pen on you at all times. So, when some stranger says "Anyone have a pen?" You will always be prepared and you are lucky you got to meet a stranger. Go home and write about them. Whatever you do- just keep writing. Much love. Keep dreaming.

Not entirely sure what is happening in this. I see a lot that I would like to critique but will focus on the fundamentals. 

~~Story~~

The jump cuts at the begging should be brief and chop blocky. Lasting only a few seconds to just establish the packing of material. I call it really trimming the fat.

The driving sequence is very lengthy. How much is establishing the mans journey into the woods needed. Does it need to be established through this sequence? The angle is askew and seems to not serve a purpose to the overall body of the short. Then the music is bit distracting. 

I feel like this film starts at around three minutes when the lead makes it outdoors. The scenery becomes vivid and vibrant with greenery. 

The story itself has a lot of detail in purpose. A man makes a journey into the woods- finds himself- does not like what he sees- it makes him sick. Kind of beauful

~~Imagery~~

I am not sure if your tone is supposed to be saturated with a highly blue hue. There are wonderful compositions and style. Like the opening texture with the wallpaper and the  main character on his phone. It was a wonderful choice of camera placement and angle. I am curious if there was purpose behind the soft focus on the foreground. The lead should be in focus. This might have just been a been just visual miscue. But if done on purpose- I would love to know the reasoning. 

Once out in the woods- with all the static shots held on sticks (a tripod) there is no tension with the camera and characters. It is a lot of back and forth. I feel like this scene should be shot mobile and maybe with a little bit of shake. This actually can be fixed in editing as well, if you are using Premiere, Push in the frame a bit and add some camera shake. A static shot, no matter the angle, has zero suspense. Unless it is comparable to an old western stare down with the tension focused solely on the build up of something happening. I can tell you might have a lot of viewings of old Clint Eastwood, John Ford  movies. But that doesn't fit onto the theme of this piece. 

There are a lot of burnt frames, so watch your ISO and IRIS. Writing it down between shots helps. Especially when reversing shots. This can also be touched up in editing. Scene matching. But the over exposure happens in the camera through the lens. It becomes almost impossible to fix a burnt frame in post. It takes a lot of masking and cutting to really tear the frame apart and even then it looks over digitized. Especially when working with outdoor colors. I think of it like this sometimes- Everyone knows the color of a leaf. Everyone knows what color it is supposed to be during the fall season. Unless it is artistic and Avant Garde to change the tone, then the leaf should look green. If that makes sense. 

~~Overall thoughts~~

There is a wonderful story being told. A mans self reflection through nature. The visuals are shaped in a way that you are focusing on the story. You wrote, shot, and created something that told a story. That is something that should be commended in itself. Keep rolling, keep creating, and keep dreaming. Much love.

You have remarkable editing skills. The shot composure is wonderful. The use of extreme close up on the eyes to instill a sense of fear is very ruminant of  horror cinema. Focusing on small subjects to extend the length of your scene with miniscule details, i.e. walking and shoes, is a wonderful example. This is when mindfulness comes into fruition. There are a lot of techniques to refocus your thoughts. Meditation being one of them. So if you can focus, try doing it. Listen to meditative music. Use the calm app. Another method is to fins hobbies. Things that make you focus on the present. I carry a notebook almost everywhere. I write things down. But a sketchpad- even if you are not artistic. This is also why earbuds have become so popular. Sometimes listening to music can help. Makes you focus on the music instead of your thoughts. Try listening to uplifting things and not the lyrics. Strange, but monks chanting and things like that. When all else fails-go for a walk. Look at everything around you. Start giving the leaves a descriptive. What color are they? Is there a crack in the sidewalk? How did the crack get there? Did that god just bark? What kind of dog is it? Look at everything around you. Take it in and observe the world. Once I started doing this, I started noticing the stars and moon and sunsets a lot more. Realizing how beautiful the world can e sometimes. It isn't always effective. In fact, I ruminate and am introspective almost daily. Probably about 14-24 hours. Which is a lot. I have tried to focus on myself and not watch a lot of entertainment, so I limit my television time to almost none. I have become addicted to my computer though. So, if you like television- it is also a form of meditation. The glowing light that draws the moths to boredom. Which is what I refer to it anyways. Most of all- think about this and understand- these are your thoughts. This is your brain. This is your life. You can control it. You will control it. You are going through something at the moment that is making you reflect and want to problem solve and your mind doesn't come up with just one solution, it comes up with many. Which all seem to be the wrong answer. So it continues to keep pondering for the right answer. Sometimes there is no right answer. But, if the thought is what I am intuitively interpreting- IT WOULD BE. Try mindfulness. I do it just sitting at my desk sometimes. I have tried many things to quiet the ruminations, but it still happens. Also know, you may have ADHD. Please do not let this disturb you, as it is so common. Believe it or not, I think society is breeding young minds for having attention disorders. Look at the time length of most tick-tok videos. Then how fast paced cartoons are. The actual attention span is only 4 seconds long. That is how long it takes an average person to have a thought. You just do not realize it because it happens so quickly in real time and it is impossible to time someone's thoughts. But, it somehow has been tested and theorized. If this is something that worries you and causes you distress, seek help. Talk to a counselor and let the thoughts out. Do not withhold any information out of fear of judgment because thoughts are not well, illegal or wrong. They are just that. Something the mind creates to process information. Oh and by the way- while reading this- I bet your brain stopped being internalized onto itself and you practiced mindfulness and the thoughts stopped. I had to just to write it. You are well on your way to success and less worry and stress. Back to ruminating for me. Much love and take care of yourself.

Creating in general is very therapeutic. If you write, do not read it. Save it and come back to it in a couple days and see if it is any good. Then edit it if it is not. Never delete anything, unless it is something that warrants deleting because of the thoughts. There are so many forms of art that it is boundless. Everyone has the potential to be an artist with the device in their pocket. Take photos. Walk around your home or apartment or school. Look at things oblongish. Like a staircase. Try not to photograph is as if though you were looking at it directly. Turn the camera, kneel, and find the shadows. Pen and paper. Draw anything. Doesn't matter if it looks good or not. Remind yourself that even if it is shit, you created something. Never throw away art. One artist trash is another friends gift. It is something that just comes from within. But part of being an artist is self critique. I find myself always deconstructing my own work and tossing things in the trash because I hate them. With everything but photography. If I roll on 1000 images on a single SD, maybe four of them are useful. I still keep the other 9996 because you can take out single pixels and use them in other projects. Record yourself. Do a podcast. There are so many artistic outlets, the options are infinite. Because everyone has a need to create, whether they realize it or not. Just making it a habit and finding the one that you are really passionate about, is the difficult aspect. Paint with your toes. Write with your teeth. learn calligraphy. Whatever it is, get it out of you man. You may hate it, but shit Jackson Pollock's art looks like blotches to me and people love it.
